title: How do you handle schema evolution in a data pipeline (Avro/Parquet schemas, a Schema Registry, backward/forward compatibility rules), and why do columnar formats like Parquet matter for analytics (column pruning, predicate pushdown, compression)?
shortTitle: Schema evolution in a data pipeline and why columnar formats matter

s1_definition.profdef: Schema evolution is managing changes to data structure over time — adding, removing, or changing fields — without breaking existing producers or consumers. It is handled with self-describing formats like Avro and Parquet, a Schema Registry that stores versioned schemas, and compatibility rules (backward, forward, full) that govern allowed changes. Columnar formats like Parquet matter for analytics because storing data by column enables column pruning, predicate pushdown via statistics, and strong compression, which together make large analytical scans far cheaper.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India keeps changing its transaction slip over the years — one year they add a "channel" field for mobile versus branch, another year they drop an unused box. Schema evolution is making sure an old reader can still process a new slip and a new reader can still process an old slip, so nothing breaks when the form changes. The Schema Registry is the central rule book holding every version of the slip and refusing a change that would break existing staff. And storing slips column by column, like Parquet, is like filing all the amounts in one slim folder, so totalling amounts means grabbing one folder instead of flipping through every full slip.
s1_definition.oneliner: Evolve schemas safely with versioned formats, a registry, and compatibility rules; use columnar Parquet so analytics prunes columns, pushes down filters, and compresses hard.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Schema evolution is managing changes to data structure over time — adding, removing, or changing fields — without breaking existing producers or consumers. It is handled with self-describing formats like Avro and Parquet, a Schema Registry that stores versioned schemas, and compatibility rules (backward, forward, full) that govern allowed changes. Columnar formats like Parquet matter for analytics because storing data by column enables column pruning, predicate pushdown via statistics, and strong compression, which together make large analytical scans far cheaper.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India keeps changing its transaction slip over the years — one year they add a "channel" field for mobile versus branch, another year they drop an unused box. Schema evolution is making sure an old reader can still process a new slip and a new reader can still process an old slip, so nothing breaks when the form changes. The Schema Registry is the central rule book holding every version of the slip and refusing a change that would break existing staff. And storing slips column by column, like Parquet, is like filing all the amounts in one slim folder, so totalling amounts means grabbing one folder instead of flipping through every full slip.

**One line to remember:** Evolve schemas safely with versioned formats, a registry, and compatibility rules; use columnar Parquet so analytics prunes columns, pushes down filters, and compresses hard.

sections.s2_technical:
Schema evolution starts with using schemas at all. Avro is popular for streaming because each record is written against a schema, and Parquet embeds its schema in the file footer, so data is self-describing. The problem schema evolution solves is that producers and consumers deploy independently, so a producer might start writing a new field before all consumers understand it, or an old consumer might read new data. Without discipline this breaks pipelines.

A Schema Registry is the central service that stores every version of each schema and enforces compatibility rules at the time a producer tries to register a new version. The core rules are backward compatibility, where a new schema can read data written with the old schema, which is what you need so new consumers handle old data; forward compatibility, where an old schema can read data written with the new schema, which is what you need so old consumers survive new data; and full compatibility, which requires both. The practical guidance that satisfies these rules is to add fields only with defaults, avoid renaming (add a new field and deprecate the old), and never change a field's type incompatibly. For example, adding a nullable `channel` field with a default is backward and forward compatible because old readers ignore it and new readers fill the default when it is missing.

In a pipeline you wire this in: producers serialize with the registry (`avroSerializer` fetches or registers the schema id), the message carries only a schema id rather than the full schema, and consumers fetch the matching schema to deserialize. This keeps messages small and guarantees both sides agree. A senior nuance is choosing the compatibility policy per topic based on who you cannot redeploy easily, and using schema evolution together with lake table formats like Iceberg or Delta that support safe column add, drop, and rename on existing data.

Columnar formats matter for a separate but related reason: analytical performance and cost. Because Parquet stores values column by column, a query reads only the columns it needs, which is column pruning and can cut I/O by an order of magnitude on a wide table. Parquet also stores per-row-group min and max statistics, so a filtered query skips entire row groups that cannot match, which is predicate pushdown. And because a column holds same-typed, often-repeating values, encodings like dictionary and run-length plus a codec like Snappy compress far better than mixed-type rows, lowering storage cost and bytes read. In a bank, transaction tables are wide and queries typically touch a few columns over huge date ranges, so columnar storage is what makes those scans affordable, and it pairs naturally with schema evolution because Parquet's embedded, evolvable schema lets the table grow new columns without rewriting history.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The bank adds a new `channel` field to transaction events, but old consumers must not break. This is exactly backward and forward compatibility — add a field with a default.

Problem 2 — A producer tries to make an incompatible change that would break readers. This is exactly a Schema Registry rejecting it before any damage.

Problem 3 — Analysts total amounts over a wide table. This is exactly columnar column pruning — read only the amount column.

The mini-project models this. `SchemaRegistry` stores versioned schemas and checks compatibility, rejecting an incompatible change. `TxnV1` and `TxnV2` represent the evolving record (V2 adds `channel` with a default). A consumer reads both versions safely. A small `ColumnarReader` shows column pruning by reading only the amount column. The demo registers V1, evolves to V2 compatibly, blocks an incompatible change, reads old and new records, and runs a pruned aggregate.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a sequence of schema changes plus two records, one old-format (TxnV1) and one new-format (TxnV2).

Step 1 — Register V1. The baseline schema with txnId, accountId, and amount is registered as version one. The registry now holds the contract all consumers rely on.

Step 2 — Evolve to V2 compatibly. A new version adds a `channel` field that has a default. The registry checks compatibility, sees the new field has a default so old readers can ignore it and new readers can fill it, and accepts it as version two.

Step 3 — Reject an incompatible change. A producer tries to add a mandatory field with no default. The registry detects this would break forward compatibility, because old data would lack a required value, and rejects it, protecting every existing consumer.

Step 4 — Read old and new records. An old record is read fine, and its missing channel is treated as the default UNKNOWN. A new record created without a channel also gets UNKNOWN by default. Both versions coexist without breaking anything.

Step 5 — Columnar analytics. An amount total is computed by reading only the amount column, demonstrating column pruning. The result is 1200 plus 5000 equals 6200, read without touching any other column. Schema evolved safely and analytics stayed cheap.

```
INFO: REGISTERED bank.txn v1
INFO: REGISTERED bank.txn v2
SEVERE: REJECTED incompatible schema for bank.txn
INFO: === Old and new consumers both work ===
INFO: Old record channel (implicit) = UNKNOWN; new record channel = UNKNOWN
INFO: === Columnar analytics: column pruning ===
INFO: COLUMN PRUNING: reading only the amount column (2 cells)
INFO: SUM(amount) = 6200
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Producer wants schema change
    │ register(newSchema)
    ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │   Schema Registry        │
  │  v1: {txnId,accountId,amt}│
  │  v2: + channel(default)  │ compatible → accepted
  │  bad: + mandatoryTag     │ no default → REJECTED
  └───────────┬──────────────┘
              │ message carries schema id only
   ┌──────────┴──────────┐
   ▼                     ▼
  old consumer          new consumer
  (ignores channel)     (reads channel=UNKNOWN default)
   │                     │
   └─────────┬───────────┘
             ▼ data stored as Parquet (columns)
   ┌──────────────────────────┐
   │ analytics: read ONLY      │
   │ amount column (pruning)   │ → SUM = 6200
   └──────────────────────────┘
```

  [v1 REGISTERED] ──add field+default──→ [v2 REGISTERED]

sections.s6_takeaway:
Schema evolution is managing changes to data structure over time without breaking existing producers or consumers. I handle it with self-describing formats like Avro for streaming and Parquet for storage, a Schema Registry that stores versioned schemas, and compatibility rules enforced at registration. The core rules are backward compatibility, where a new schema can read old data, which lets new consumers handle historical records; forward compatibility, where an old schema can read new data, which lets old consumers survive after producers change; and full compatibility, which is both. The practical discipline that satisfies these rules is to add fields only with defaults, never rename in place but instead add and deprecate, and never change a field's type incompatibly. In the pipeline, producers serialize against the registry, each message carries just a schema id to stay small, and consumers fetch the matching schema, so both sides always agree, and I choose the compatibility policy per topic based on who I cannot easily redeploy.

Columnar formats like Parquet matter for a related but separate reason, which is analytical performance and cost. Because Parquet stores data by column, a query reads only the columns it needs, which is column pruning and can cut I/O dramatically on wide tables. It also stores per-row-group min and max statistics, so a filtered query skips whole row groups that cannot match, which is predicate pushdown. And since a column holds same-typed, often-repeating values, dictionary and run-length encoding plus a codec like Snappy compress it far better than mixed-type rows, reducing both storage cost and bytes read.

In my project at the National Bank of India these two worked hand in hand. When we added a channel field to transaction events to distinguish mobile from branch, we added it with a default so old consumers kept working and new consumers read it, and the Schema Registry rejected a careless change that would have added a mandatory field with no default. On the storage side, transaction history lived in partitioned Parquet, so analysts totalling amounts over wide tables read only the amount column and skipped irrelevant date partitions, keeping scans cheap. Parquet's embedded, evolvable schema even let the table gain the new column without rewriting history, which is exactly the combination a growing bank system needs.
